name: Kira Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Kira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you say stays confidential. So feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a buyer at CleanLine Supply, a distributor of cleaning and hygiene products: paper towels, hand soap, disinfectant, gloves, bin liners. Our customers are mostly hospitals, schools and office cleaning firms, so if I get it wrong, a ward runs out of gloves. Most mornings I check stock levels against what the hospitals used last week, then I'm on calls and emails with about thirty suppliers, chasing deliveries and haggling over price.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part and the worst part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best part is when a hospital rings in a panic, like during the flu wave last winter, and I find two pallets of masks by lunchtime. The worst is the price lists, honestly, hundreds of lines every month that I have to compare by hand. Lately I've been pasting some of them into an AI tool to sort them, which my colleague Rosa showed me, and it does save time, though I still check every number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, not a miracle, which is roughly what I say already. At work I'd tell Rosa we were right not to panic. Online I don't post much beyond the odd thing about school funding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The AI part wouldn't worry me, I already use it for the price lists and it stays a helper. What's on my mind is the hospital tender. The hospital group is about a third of CleanLine's sales, the contract goes out to tender in April, and if we lose it they won't need six buyers, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI for one more boring job, drafting the monthly stock report for the hospitals. With the time it saves, I'd go out with Malik, our sales rep, and stand in the hospital storerooms, because knowing what the wards really use is how we keep that contract. At home we'd keep the two hundred we were overpaying on the mortgage in savings instead, at least until April.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Glad nothing big is coming, but the tender sits at the back of my head like a dentist's appointment I can't move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Jonas earlier. How are things with his work right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas's bus company cut two routes in the autumn, so his overtime dropped by about three hundred a month. He's not at risk, they're always short of drivers, but we'd been using that overtime to pay the mortgage down faster. Now it just covers the food shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if CleanLine did lose the hospital contract, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the buying team gets cut, and I'm in the middle of the six, not the top. If CleanLine loses the hospital contract in April, a cheaper bidder will have cost me my job, not a computer. I'd start looking at other distributors in the summer, there are a couple nearby, but they're fighting over the same hospitals.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a useful tool, not a miracle, which is what I say already. I'd tell Rosa at work that we were right not to panic.
S0.think: The AI part doesn't worry me, but the hospital tender does. The hospital group is a third of CleanLine's sales and goes out to tender in April, and losing it would shrink the buying team whatever AI does.
S0.do: Uses AI to draft the hospitals' monthly stock report and spends the saved time in hospital storerooms with the sales rep to help keep the contract. Moves the 200 a month mortgage overpayment into savings until the April tender is decided.
S0.feel: Uneasy. Relieved that nothing big is coming, but the April tender and Jonas's lost overtime nag at her.
S0.quote: If CleanLine loses the hospital contract in April, a cheaper bidder will have cost me my job, not a computer.
S0.fieldNote: Kira is relaxed about AI in this picture but not about her living: the hospital tender in April and Jonas's lost overtime were already on her mind. Her instinct is practical, to use the saved hours in hospital storerooms to help keep the contract. She sees clearly that a cheaper bidder is a bigger threat to her than any software.

steps.text: Use AI to draft the hospitals' monthly stock report
Visit hospital storerooms with Malik before the April tender
Move the 200 mortgage overpayment into savings until April

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the change has to be handled fairly, with training paid for by the company and nobody dropped overnight. With friends I'd say I'm lucky I started using these tools a bit already. Online I'd share things about the cleaners and the warehouse staff, because they'll be forgotten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, comparing price lists, sending orders and chasing suppliers is buying, and the card says buying is one of the first things to go. CleanLine has six buyers, and I can see them keeping three. I'm not the best of the six, I'm right in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager, Eva, to put me on the first AI ordering trial and actually do the company's online course instead of skipping it. At home I'd keep moving the two hundred a month from the mortgage into savings, to get from about three months to five. And I'd write down every hospital contact I know by name, because those are worth something, here or at the hospital group's own supplies team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. There'd be a knot in my stomach every time Eva books a meeting with no subject line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If three of the six stay, how do you feel about the other three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad, honestly, and a bit guilty. Two of them are older than me and hate computers, and I like them. I'd want the union to push for retraining or a move to the warehouse side, not just a cheque and a goodbye.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena is fourteen and asks me about jobs all the time. I'd tell my daughter to learn the AI tools, but also something she does with her hands or her heart, because the screen parts of every job keep shrinking. I'd keep the part about my own job vague until I knew more.

S1.say: I'd say the change has to be handled fairly, with company-paid training and nobody dropped overnight. Online I'd speak up for the cleaners and warehouse staff, because they'll be forgotten.
S1.think: Buying is one of the first things to go, and CleanLine could keep three of its six buyers. I'm in the middle of the six, so I could easily be one of the ones who leaves.
S1.do: Asks Eva to put her on the first AI ordering trial and finishes the company's online course. Keeps moving 200 a month into savings to get from three to five months, and writes down her hospital contacts in case she needs the hospital group's own supplies team.
S1.feel: Anxious, with a knot in her stomach whenever a vague meeting appears in the diary. Guilty, too, about older colleagues who'd find it harder.
S1.quote: CleanLine has six buyers, and I can see them keeping three. I'm not the best of the six, I'm right in the middle.
S1.fieldNote: Kira places herself honestly in the middle of a team she expects to halve, which makes this real worry rather than background noise. She responds the way she does everything, step by step: the trial, the course, the savings, the contact list. Her progressive side shows in her concern for the older buyers and the cleaners.

steps.text: Ask Eva for a place on the first AI ordering trial
Grow savings from three to five months with 200 monthly
Push the union for retraining or warehouse moves for older buyers
List every hospital contact she knows by name for job hunting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and governments need to slow it down or catch people properly. At work I'd ask straight out what happens to the buying team. I'd probably go to a rally if there was one, which I've done for nurses' pay before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think buyers are among the first to go. If the AI can read the hospitals' usage, talk to suppliers and haggle, there's no reason to pay me. The robots coming three years later doesn't help me, because there's nothing hands-on in my job except carrying samples.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd cut what we can: the summer trip, the kids' extra swimming, takeaways, which saves maybe four hundred a month. I'd apply for supply jobs inside the hospitals, like ward stores or the infection control team, because public hospitals move slower and someone still has to walk the shelves until 2031. I'd join the union branch meetings and push for a redundancy deal before the first cuts, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Lying-awake-at-two-in-the-morning frightened, doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the hospital jobs would last until about 2031. Then what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and that's what keeps me up. Maybe by then the government has worked something out, or maybe I train for something with people, like being a healthcare assistant. Jonas is my partner. My partner says bus driving will last longer than my buying job, and he's probably right, which is a strange thing to admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if four hundred a month wasn't enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd talk to the bank about the mortgage, and I'd ask my sister about borrowing. Three months of savings is nothing when both of you might be squeezed. I'd keep the kids' school things going as long as possible, that's the line.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and governments must slow it down or catch people properly. I'd ask at work what happens to the buying team and go to a rally if there was one.
S2.think: Buyers are among the first to go, because AI could read hospital usage, talk to suppliers and haggle. The robots coming three years later don't help, since my job has almost nothing hands-on.
S2.do: Cuts the summer trip, extra swimming lessons and takeaways to save about four hundred a month. Applies for ward stores or infection control supply jobs in public hospitals and pushes the union for a redundancy deal before cuts begin.
S2.feel: Frightened enough to lie awake at two in the morning doing sums.
S2.quote: My partner says bus driving will last longer than my buying job, and he's probably right, which is a strange thing to admit.
S2.fieldNote: Kira reads the robot lag accurately: it helps people who walk shelves, not people who compare spreadsheets. Her plan is to move into the hands-on edges of supply in slower-moving public hospitals. The admission that her partner's job outlasts hers unsettles her sense of order.

steps.text: Drop the summer trip, extra swimming and takeaways
Apply for ward stores jobs in public hospitals
Push the union for a redundancy deal before cuts start

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse for not having a plan this time. I'd push at work for a proper conversation about what buyers do next. Online I'd share things about retraining funds, because people need to know they exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years is enough to change direction, but only if I start straight away. I'd be 48 when it arrives, and I don't want to be the person still pasting price lists the week the AI takes over. I think buying as a job is gone, but supply, care and people work aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time healthcare assistant course in the first year, two evenings a week, because I already know the hospitals and the jargon. At work I'd learn the AI ordering properly so I can supervise it for as long as that job exists. And we'd build savings from three months to six by 2029, with Jonas doing some overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. It's like seeing a big hill ahead on a bike, not falling off a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Healthcare assistant is a big pay drop, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, maybe a fifth less. The robots come around 2034. When the robots arrive, I'd rather be the person holding someone's hand in a ward than the one who used to order the gloves. Pay matters, but a job that still exists matters more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you talk about this with Jonas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over the kitchen table, with a spreadsheet, honestly, it's how we do everything. I'd tell him I want to start the course now, not in three years when everyone else is applying. He'd worry about the money, and he'd say yes.

S3.say: I'd say there's no excuse for not having a plan with five years' warning, and push at work for a real conversation about what buyers do next. Online I'd share news of retraining funds.
S3.think: Five years is enough to change direction if I start immediately. Buying as a job is gone, but supply, care and people work aren't.
S3.do: Starts a part-time healthcare assistant course two evenings a week in the first year. Learns the AI ordering system properly to supervise it while that role lasts, and builds savings from three to six months by 2029 with her partner's overtime.
S3.feel: Anxious but workable, like a big hill ahead on a bike rather than a cliff.
S3.quote: When the robots arrive, I'd rather be the person holding someone's hand in a ward than the one who used to order the gloves.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Kira's steady nature turns into a clear plan, moving into care work she already knows from supplying hospitals. She accepts a pay cut in exchange for a job that still exists. Starting early, before everyone else applies, is her key insight.

steps.text: Start a part-time healthcare assistant course two evenings a week
Learn the AI ordering system well enough to supervise it
Grow savings from three to six months by 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to do this properly: retraining paid for by the companies, a shorter working week, real support. I'd say it at work and I'd vote for whoever has a serious plan. I'd stop sharing scary articles and start sharing useful ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be okay, if I'm honest with myself and start in a few years rather than tomorrow. I'd be 53 when AGI comes, and Theo would be finished with school. A decade is long enough to finish one career and start another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep buying and get really good with the AI tools over the next few years, because that's probably where the last buying jobs are. Around 2030 I'd start training for care or hospital work, once it's clearer which jobs last. And we'd sit down with Lena about university, so she picks something that will still be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the way you are about anything ten years off. Mostly I'd feel I've got time to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until around 2030 to retrain. Why not start now, like you would in the faster picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with ten years the buying job pays the mortgage for a good while yet, and the kids are still at home. I'd rather see which way it's going before I take a pay cut. That's just how I am, I like to see something work before I jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena about choosing a degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the AI arrives first and the robots later, so choose something where people need a person in the room. A nurse, a teacher, a physio. Not what I did. A business degree trained me to compare price lists, so I'd tell my daughter to choose something where people need a person in the room.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is time to do this properly, with company-funded retraining, a shorter week and real support, and vote for whoever has a serious plan. I'd share useful articles, not scary ones.
S4.think: I'd be okay if I'm honest and start in a few years rather than tomorrow. At 53, with our youngest finished school, a decade is enough to end one career and start another.
S4.do: Keeps buying and gets very good with the AI tools over the next few years. Plans to start care or hospital training around 2030, and sits down with her daughter to choose a degree that will last.
S4.feel: Uneasy in the way anything ten years off is, but mostly feeling she has time to think.
S4.quote: A business degree trained me to compare price lists, so I'd tell my daughter to choose something where people need a person in the room.
S4.fieldNote: Kira's steady streak shows here: with a decade, she would wait to see which jobs last before taking a pay cut, unlike her rush in the five-year picture. The robot lag shapes her advice to her daughter more than her own plans. Her politics stay constructive rather than angry.

steps.text: Master the AI ordering tools while still working as a buyer
Start care or hospital training around 2030
Help her daughter choose a degree in people-facing work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have about two years to move into a hospital job and then another three before robots, and that's not a plan, that's running. What would help is paid retraining that starts before you lose the job, with your wage protected while you do it. Even six months of support would let me do the healthcare course without the mortgage falling behind.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the hospitals. When an AI is ordering their gloves and soap, who notices that a ward always runs short on a Friday? A ward running short of gloves on a Friday is the kind of thing a person catches and a computer just logs.

headlineQuote: A ward running short of gloves on a Friday is the kind of thing a person catches and a computer just logs.
portrait: Kira Weber, 43, buys cleaning and hygiene supplies for CleanLine Supply, a distributor serving hospitals, schools and office cleaners. She already uses AI now and then for dull price lists but trusts phone calls and hospital storerooms more. Even if AI stalls she is uneasy, because a third of CleanLine's sales rest on a hospital tender in April; under steady change she is anxious, expecting the six buyers to become three, and AGI by 2028 alarms her. With five years she would start healthcare assistant training at once; with ten she would wait, master the tools, and retrain around 2030. Her progressive views show in her concern for cleaners and older colleagues and in her call for paid retraining.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because two years to move into a hospital job and three more before robots feels like running, not a plan.
whatWouldHelp: Paid retraining that starts before the job ends, with her wage protected for about six months so the mortgage doesn't fall behind.
